190.title: Al-Layl: the giver
190.hook: the one who gives and guards himself, We ease him toward ease (92:5–7)
190.tomorrow: Ash-Shams: the sun and her brightness
190.howItsDone: Many Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, quietly and without being asked, alongside the obligatory zakat; the closing verses of Al-Layl are often recalled as the picture of giving for God's sake alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Layl, the night, and efforts that go in different directions. Your line was efforts differ.

The bill lands on the table, and one friend has already paid it before anyone else has noticed. The same friend drops off soup when someone's sick, without asking whether they want soup. For her, giving looks like breathing. For someone else at the same table, there's a tight little hesitation before handing anything over, the math running in the head. Same table, same bill, two different reflexes. Now Al-Layl names the two directions, and makes a claim about which one gets easier with time.
screen: `THE ONE WHO PICKS UP THE BILL.` → `THE TIGHT LITTLE HESITATION.` → `TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Right after the oaths, the surah draws two portraits. The first, verses five to seven: the one who gives, who is mindful of God, and who affirms what is good. Then, in Pickthall's words: Surely We will ease his way unto the state of ease. The second, verses eight to ten, is the mirror: the one who holds back, who thinks he needs no one, and who denies the good. For him, the way is eased toward hardship. The words are al-yusra and al-'usra, ease and hardship, from the same two roots as the pair in Ash-Sharh a few days ago: with hardship comes ease. Here they become directions of travel. And the verb is the same for both men: We will ease him. Both are eased. The road smooths out for each of them, just toward different places. Giving makes giving easier; holding back makes holding back easier. Near its end, the surah returns to the giver. Verses seventeen to twenty-one describe the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, not to repay a favor anyone did him, seeking only the face of his Lord, the Most High. The last line of the surah is a promise: he will be content. Some commentators report that these closing verses were revealed about Abu Bakr, who spent his money buying the freedom of enslaved believers, Bilal among them. That's a report in the tafsir, not in the text. The text leaves the giver unnamed, so anyone can fit.
screen: `TWO PORTRAITS: GIVE, OR HOLD BACK.` · `YUSRA AND 'USRA — EASE AND HARDSHIP.` · `BOTH ROADS GET EASIER.` · `GIVING WITH NOTHING OWED.` · then, large: `GIVING MAKES IT EASY.`

segments.voice: Think of the people around you this week, and let one come to mind who could use something and hasn't asked: a message, a meal, a ride, some time. Picture giving it before they ask, and notice where the hesitation shows up in your body, if it does. Then decide what you'll give, and when.
Al-Layl. The night, Surah ninety-two: the giver is eased toward ease, and the one who holds back toward hardship. Today's word.
Your line: giving makes it easy. A road smooths out the more it's walked. That's day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Ash-Shams: the sun and her brightness
191.hook: eleven oaths by sun, moon, day, night, sky and earth (91:1–7)
191.howItsDone: Ash-Shams is one of the short surahs often recited in the prayer, especially the evening and night prayers; many Muslims learn its run of oaths by heart as children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Layl and the giver, eased toward ease. Your line was giving makes it easy.

When did you last watch the sun actually go down? Not a glance through a windshield. The whole slow slide: the light going orange, then pink, the sky still glowing after the sun itself is gone. Most people see about a hundred sunsets a year and look at maybe two. Ash-Shams, the surah before Al-Layl, won't let you skip it. It opens with a string of oaths, one after another, and every one points at something you walk under every day and mostly ignore.
screen: `A HUNDRED SUNSETS A YEAR.` → `MOST LOOK AT MAYBE TWO.` → `ASH-SHAMS, THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-one begins, in Pickthall's translation: By the sun and his brightness. In Arabic the sun, shams, is grammatically feminine, which is why the title says her brightness; Pickthall's English says his. The word for brightness, duha, you already know: it names the morning surah from a few days ago, the full light of mid-morning. Then the oaths keep coming. By the moon when it follows the sun. By the day when it shows the sun's glory. By the night when it covers it. By the sky and the One who built it. By the earth and the One who spread it out. By the soul and the One who shaped it. Commentators count eleven things sworn by, more than in any other surah. Why swear at all? In Arabic, an oath says: stop, look at this, what comes next matters. The things sworn by are witnesses. And look at the order. It starts huge and far away, the sun, and moves steadily closer: moon, day and night, sky, earth, and last, the soul. The whole universe, and then you, like a camera zooming from space down to a single face. Where the zoom lands is tomorrow's lesson. Today is the zoom itself: the ordinary sky is worth an oath. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once told a companion who was making the night prayer too long for the people behind him to recite shorter surahs, and a hadith in Muslim's collection names Ash-Shams among them. Short enough for a tired crowd, big enough to hold the whole sky.

segments.voice: Wherever you are, find the light: a window, a patch of sun on the floor, the glow of the sky. Look at it for a while, its color, where it falls, how it changes things. If it's night, picture the last sunset you remember, as clearly as you can.

Your line: by the sun. Eleven witnesses, and the first one is overhead every day. Tomorrow, where the zoom lands.

192.title: Ash-Shams: the soul
192.hook: by the soul and its shaping, successful is the one who purifies it (91:7–10)
192.carry: the one who purifies it succeeds
192.howItsDone: Muslims speak of tazkiyah, the lifelong work of purifying the soul, through prayer, remembrance, charity and watching one's habits; the verse on success in Ash-Shams is often quoted about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Shams, and a run of oaths from the sun down through the sky and the earth. Your line was by the sun.

Sun. Moon. Day. Night. Sky. Earth. And then the last thing Ash-Shams swears by, something small enough to fit inside a person. Not a star, not a mountain. A soul. Yours, and everyone's. The whole sky was the windup. After all that, the surah says one thing about the soul, one sentence about what success actually is. It isn't the kind of success that goes on a resume or into a headline.
screen: `SUN, MOON, SKY, EARTH.` → `NOT A STAR. A SOUL.` → `WHAT SUCCESS ACTUALLY IS.`

segments.voice: Verse seven: by the soul, nafs, and the One who shaped it and made it well-proportioned. Verse eight: and inspired it with its wickedness and its mindfulness. Both, in the same soul, from the start. The surah doesn't pretend people are pure by default, or rotten by default. The soul knows both roads. Then the sentence the oaths were building to, in Pickthall's words: He is indeed successful who causeth it to grow. And the next verse, the mirror: the one who buries it, who stunts it, has failed. The Arabic verb for the first is zakkaha. You've heard the root: zakat, the giving that is one of the five pillars. Z-k-y carries two ideas at once, to purify and to grow, the way pruning a plant cleans it and makes it grow stronger. Zakat purifies wealth, and this verse says a person can do the same to a soul. The opposite verb, dassaha, means to bury something, to hide it in the dirt. Later scholars gave the work of the first verb a name: tazkiyah, purification of the soul. But the verse itself is plain. Success here isn't money or followers. It's what you did with the soul you were given: did you tend it, or bury it? The surah then ends with a short, sharp story: the people of Thamud, who hamstrung the she-camel they'd been warned to leave alone. A soul buried, a whole people at a time.
screen: `THE SOUL KNOWS BOTH ROADS.` · `ZAKKAHA — TO PURIFY AND TO GROW.` · `DASSAHA — TO BURY IT IN THE DIRT.` · `SUCCESS: WHAT YOU DID WITH IT.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO PURIFIES IT SUCCEEDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one small habit that clouds your day a little: the scroll before sleep, the sharp reply, the thing you say about a coworker. Picture pruning it, one cut, not a whole new life, and see what the cut would look like. If you pray, you can ask for help with it in your own words.

Your line: the one who purifies it succeeds. Tending is done in small cuts. One hundred ninety-two days in.

193.title: Al-Balad: the steep path
193.hook: he has not attempted the steep path: freeing a slave, feeding in hunger (90:11–16)
193.tomorrow: Al-Balad: two eyes, a tongue, two lips
193.howItsDone: Many Muslims give food to the hungry as sadaqah, especially to poor relatives and orphans, and support charities that pay off debts or free people from bondage, reading these verses of Al-Balad as a description of the harder road.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Shams, and the soul that can be tended or buried. Your line was the one who purifies it succeeds.
screen: `ASH-SHAMS — THE ONE WHO PURIFIES IT SUCCEEDS.`

segments.voice: Halfway up a mountain, the trail forks. One way is the switchback path, long and gentle, crowded with people in sneakers. The other goes straight up, rocks and roots, the kind of climb where the legs start arguing before the first step. The gentle one is the easy pick, and nobody blames anyone for taking it. Al-Balad, the city, the surah before Ash-Shams, uses this picture, a hard mountain road, and then asks a question that sounds like a riddle: do you know what the steep path is? The answer isn't a mountain at all.
screen: `THE TRAIL FORKS.` → `GENTLE, OR STRAIGHT UP?` → `WHAT IS THE STEEP PATH?`

segments.voice: Surah ninety opens with an oath by this city, al-balad, which commentators take to be Mecca, the Prophet's own city, where he and his followers were being made unwelcome. Then it describes a certain kind of person, loud about the money he's spent, sure nobody sees him. Verse eleven, in Pickthall's words: But he hath not attempted the Ascent. The Arabic is al-'aqabah, a steep mountain pass, the kind of road that makes you lean forward and use your hands. Then the riddle: what will tell you what the steep path is? The answer comes in verses thirteen to sixteen. Freeing a neck, meaning freeing someone who is enslaved. Feeding, on a day of hunger, an orphan who is a relative, or a poor person lying in the dust. That's the mountain. Not a spiritual feat, not a vision. Setting someone free, and feeding someone hungry. Why is that steep? Because it costs. The man at the start of the surah spent plenty, and bragged about it. The steep path is spending where nobody claps: on a relative you're a little tired of helping, on a stranger in the dust. Verse seventeen adds one more step: to be among those who believe and who urge each other to patience and to compassion. The climb isn't done alone; people on the steep path pull each other up. In the Prophet's time, freeing an enslaved person was a real and costly act, and the Qur'an names it again in Surah nine, verse sixty, among the uses of charity, next to helping those in debt. Some readers today also hear in this verse a call to free people from other kinds of bondage.

segments.voice: Think about food, and who near you might be hungry, or just tired of cooking for themselves: a neighbor, a relative, a coworker who skips lunch, someone you pass on the street. Choose one person, and one way you could feed them: a meal, a coffee, a donation to a food bank.

194.title: Al-Balad: two eyes, a tongue, two lips
194.hook: have We not given him two eyes, a tongue and lips, and shown him two ways (90:8–10)
194.tomorrow: Al-Fajr: the dawn and ten nights
194.howItsDone: Muslims often recall these verses of Al-Balad when speaking of guarding the tongue, a theme that runs through many hadith, and of gratitude for the senses as gifts that come with responsibility.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Balad, and the climb it names: freeing someone, feeding the hungry. Your line was take the steep path.

Try this. Touch your eyelids, gently. Then your lips. Then press your tongue against the back of your teeth. All three have been busy all day, mostly without a thought: reading this screen, talking to the barista, tasting the coffee, muttering at the traffic. Equipment doesn't get more ordinary than this. Right before the steep path, Al-Balad stops and points at exactly this equipment, and asks a question about it. Then it adds one more gift that you can't touch at all.
screen: `TOUCH YOUR EYELIDS. YOUR LIPS.` → `EVERYDAY EQUIPMENT.` → `ONE GIFT YOU CAN'T TOUCH.`

segments.voice: Al-Balad describes a man who boasts that he has spent heaps of money and thinks no one sees him. The surah answers with a question, verse eight, in Pickthall's words: Did We not assign unto him two eyes, and a tongue and two lips? The man who thinks no one sees him was given the power to see. The man bragging with his mouth was given the mouth. It's a gentle, almost funny reversal: everything he's using to show off was handed to him. Why two lips, and not just a mouth? Some commentators notice that lips close. The tongue can speak, and the lips can hold it back; the same equipment can say the cruel thing or keep it in. Then verse ten: and We showed him the two ways. The Arabic is an-najdayn, the two raised roads, the two highland paths. Ibn Kathir gives the common reading: the way of good and the way of harm, both shown clearly, like two roads on a ridge you can see from far off. He also reports a few who read it more tenderly, as the two sources of milk a newborn is guided to without being taught. Either way, guidance was given before you asked for it. Eyes to see the roads, a tongue to speak on the good one, lips to stop at the other. Then verse eleven, from yesterday: but he did not attempt the steep path. So the surah's logic runs: you were given the tools, you were shown the roads, now climb.

195.title: Al-Fajr: the dawn and ten nights
195.hook: by the dawn and ten nights, taken as the first ten of Dhul Hijjah (89:1–2)
195.howItsDone: Muslims pray fajr, the dawn prayer, in the first light before sunrise; in the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah many fast, give charity and say the takbir often, taking these as the ten nights of Surah 89.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Balad, with its eyes, tongue and lips, and the two roads shown. Your line was two roads shown.

Five in the morning has its own kind of quiet. The streetlights are still on. The birds start before the traffic does. New parents know that hour, and early-shift workers, and anyone with a flight to catch, usually by accident. For Muslims who pray, it's the start of the day on purpose: the first of the five daily prayers is named for that hour, and comes before the sun is up. Al-Fajr, the surah just before Al-Balad, opens by swearing by it.
screen: `FIVE IN THE MORNING.` → `THE BIRDS BEFORE THE TRAFFIC.` → `AL-FAJR, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-nine opens, in Pickthall's words: By the Dawn And ten nights. Fajr comes from a root for breaking open, bursting through; the Qur'an uses the same root in Surah seventeen for a spring gushing out of the ground. Dawn is the moment light breaks through the dark. It's also the name of the first daily prayer, prayed in the gray light before sunrise, when many people are still asleep. And ten nights. Which ten? The surah doesn't say. The reading Ibn Kathir prefers, which he traces to Ibn Abbas, is the first ten nights of Dhul Hijjah, the month of the Hajj, the days leading up to the pilgrimage's high point and the feast of Eid al-Adha. Others said the last ten nights of Ramadan, and some the first ten of Muharram. The text itself leaves it open. Those who take the Dhul Hijjah reading point to a hadith in Bukhari: no good deeds done on other days are better than those done in these ten. So those days are kept with extra fasting, giving, and saying Allahu akbar, even far from Mecca. Then more oaths: by the even and the odd, by the night as it moves on. And a question: is there not in this an oath for someone with sense? The word for sense, hijr, means something that holds you back, a check, like a wall. The oaths are for the person whose mind can stop and notice. A dawn, some nights, a question: the first of four days with this surah.

196.title: Al-Fajr: the old cities
196.hook: 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh built high and went too far (89:6–13)
196.howItsDone: Muslims read the Qur'an's accounts of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh as lessons about pride and power; many who visit ancient ruins recall these verses and reflect on the peoples who built them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fajr, the dawn, and ten nights nobody can quite pin down. Your line was by the dawn.

Every big city has one: the tower built to be the tallest, the name on the side in letters you can read from the highway. And every traveler has stood somewhere else, among broken columns in a desert or a jungle, reading a sign that says a great city stood here, and wondering what the people thought when they built it. Did they think it would last? The second passage of Al-Fajr takes the listener on exactly that kind of tour, through three peoples who built high.
screen: `THE TOWER WITH ITS NAME ON THE SIDE.` → `BROKEN COLUMNS IN THE DESERT.` → `THE OLD CITIES.`

segments.voice: Verse six asks: have you not seen what your Lord did with 'Ad? Then three stops. First, 'Ad, and Iram, the city of pillars, whose like was never made in any land. 'Ad were an ancient Arabian people; their prophet, the Qur'an says elsewhere, was Hud. People have searched for Iram for centuries, and nobody knows for certain where it stood. Second, Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley. Their prophet was Salih. Muslims have long connected them with al-Hijr in northwest Arabia, where huge facades are cut into sandstone; archaeologists date those carvings to the Nabataeans, a later people, so the link is tradition, not settled history. Third, Pharaoh, lord of the stakes. Commentators read the stakes as the pegs of great tents or armies, or as monuments fixed firmly in the ground, or as a way he punished people. All three, verse eleven says, overstepped in the land and multiplied corruption. Then, in Pickthall's words: Lo! thy Lord is ever watchful. The Arabic is bil-mirsad, on the lookout, like a watchtower on a road. Here's the irony: these were builders of pillars and towers and monuments, and the real watchtower was never theirs. The Qur'an isn't against building. It's against building as a way of saying I don't answer to anyone. That ends a week: Al-Layl's giver eased toward ease, then the sun, and the soul that can be tended or buried, then the steep path and the two roads, then the dawn. Today, the towers.

segments.voice: Think of something built to impress: a skyscraper, a stadium, a mansion online, or something of your own, a resume, a profile, a car. Picture it a thousand years from now, sand, grass, a sign for tourists. Without gloom, notice what would still matter about the people who lived there.
